stories.why_it_matters: Selective capital means weaker operators will face higher funding costs or stalled deals, while those with contracted capacity, secured power and credible customers can still raise money on good terms. The bar for new market entrants has effectively risen, likely consolidating advantage with established platforms.
stories.content:
AirTrunk and Iren, two of the country’s most valuable data centre and artificial intelligence infrastructure operators, say investors are becoming more discerning and favouring companies with strong records amid growing concern about bulging debts and sky-high valuations.

Surging borrowing costs and fears that ambitious expansion plans can’t be delivered have already foiled plans for a $44 billion listing of Firmus Technologies, with the corporate regulator disclosing that it was “undertaking inquiries” into the failure of the float this month.

stories.why_it_matters: A 40% single-stock wipeout sends a warning to every APAC operator betting on AI demand: social licence and grid approvals can now move market value as much as contracts. Developers may shift toward quieter sites, earlier community engagement, or behind-the-meter power strategies to de-risk similar exposure.

# Australian data center operator NextDC shares fall 40% after power backlash

Forecasts slashed after community opposition stalls AI expansion plans

NextDC has data centers in Australia, including this Sydney collaboration with OpenAI, New Zealand, Malaysia and Japan. © Getty Images

SHAUN TURTON

October 21, 2026 15:04 JST

CANBERRA -- Major Australian data center operator NextDC's shares tumbled 40% on Wednesday after the company revealed that a public backlash had stalled plans to increase power supply to a flagship site in Melbourne, underscoring the challenges facing the rollout of in-demand artificial intelligence infrastructure.

# Thailand fast-tracks data center rules for trillion baht investments

Thailand is accelerating regulatory guidelines for data center businesses. This aims to provide clarity on land use, infrastructure, and community safety standards for over 1 trillion baht in investments.

- Published On Oct 21, 2026 at 11:00 AM IST

## Highlights

- Thailand is accelerating regulatory guidelines for data center businesses.
- Investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure, and community safety standards.
- Projects worth over 1 trillion baht (US$30 billion) await regulatory approval.
- New rules aim to classify data centers, affecting construction and operational conditions.

stories.title: Thailand moves to finalise data center rules amid trillion baht investment pipeline
stories.summary: Thailand is accelerating work on regulatory guidelines for data center businesses as investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure requirements and community safety standards. The Data Center Policy Committee is scheduled to meet and address outstanding issues, with a draft framework expected to take shape in the first quarter of 2027. The Ministry of Digital […]
stories.why_it_matters: A Q1 2027 draft date gives investors a concrete timeline to plan around, replacing open-ended uncertainty. Developers waiting on Thai entry can now sequence land deals and power applications, while neighbouring markets competing for the same capital must assume Thailand's trillion-baht pipeline starts converting to real projects.
stories.content:
Thailand is accelerating work on regulatory guidelines for data center businesses as investors await clarity on land use, infrastructure requirements and community safety standards. The Data Center Policy Committee is scheduled to meet and address outstanding issues, with a draft framework expected to take shape in the first quarter of 2027.

The Ministry of Digital Economy and Society is working with the Big Data Institute to develop the TH-DC Dashboard, which will consolidate information on investment projects and infrastructure requirements. Four subcommittees are also reviewing economic policy, data integration, infrastructure, land use and urban planning to establish common regulatory standards according to an article by Bangkokbiznews.

Nan Boonthida Somchai, Digital Economy and Society, Deputy Minister, revealed that the main challenge is determining how data centers should be classified under industrial and urban planning regulations. The classification will influence where facilities can be built and the conditions they must meet, particularly regarding electricity, water, telecommunications infrastructure and environmental safety.

Proposed community safety requirements include minimum distances between data centers and residential areas, schools, hospitals and temples, based on the volume of fuel stored on site. Facilities storing between 90,000 and 180,000 liters would need to maintain a distance of at least 100 meters, while those storing between 180,000 and 500,000 liters would require at least 200 meters. The proposals remain under review and would form part of a wider licensing assessment.

The government faces pressure to finalise the framework as projects worth more than 1 trillion baht (US$ 30 billion) are awaiting regulatory clarity, according to investment plans held by the Board of Investment. Affected projects include operational facilities, developments under construction that lack some required approvals, particularly for electricity use, and proposed investments that have yet to begin construction.

The new guidelines are not expected to apply retroactively to existing projects. However, operators must continue to meet existing legal requirements, including regulations covering fuel storage, electricity consumption and telecommunications connections.

The government is seeking to strengthen Thailand’s position as a regional digital infrastructure and AI hub, but prolonged regulatory uncertainty could prompt investors to redirect projects to other markets.

According to an ICT market analysis from Mordor Intelligence, Thailand’s ICT market is projected to grow from US$ 17.74 billion in 2025 to US$ 33.08 billion by 2031, at a 10.95 percent CAGR. Growth is driven by nationwide 5G expansion, hyperscale data-center investments, government cloud-first initiatives, Industry 4.0 modernization, rising cybersecurity demand, and fintech development.

stories.title: AI demand reshapes data center power, grid, and supply chains
stories.summary: Machine-generated web requests surpassed human traffic for the first time in June, according to Cloudflare data, driving a shift from north-south to east-west traffic between agents and data centers. This trend highlights increasing constraints on power, grid timelines, equipment, and skilled labour within the data center industry.
stories.content:
The data center industry is grappling with new challenges as artificial intelligence (AI) demand redefines infrastructure requirements, with machine-generated web page requests now exceeding human traffic. This shift, noted at Capacity Europe 2026, necessitates changes in network architecture and supply chain planning.Cloudflare data for June showed machine-generated web page requests at 57.4 per cent, surpassing human requests for the first time. Colt chief strategy officer Avijit Singh projected that machine traffic could increase by 100 times within five years, transforming traffic flows from cloud-to-user to inter-data centre communication. This transition demands higher latency, resilience, automation, and observability, while shifting security focus towards verifying machine identity.
### Inference and Edge Computing

The industry is increasingly focused on AI inference workloads, which are now matching training investments, according to Verizon's Jeff Hulse, citing McKinsey research. Orange Wholesale's Valerie Cussac noted that AI workloads are already impacting networks, particularly between data centres. This has revived interest in edge computing, with T Wholesale's Dimitrios Rizoulis observing high demand for edge locations in Europe. DE-CIX CEO Ivo Ivanov stated that each millisecond of latency equates to approximately 80 kilometres, positioning agentic AI applications within 100 to 150 kilometres of their inference processing. Meta, which has deployed edge sites since 2013, called the industry's earlier retreat from edge a "major missed opportunity," noting current scarcity in edge capacity.
### Connectivity and Supply Chain Bottlenecks

Connectivity planning often occurs too late in data centre builds, Digital Realty's Paula Cogan said, emphasising the need for a deep connectivity ecosystem. Colt's Joe Scattareggia mentioned that new fibre builds take 12 to 18 months, with Equinix planning connectivity five years in advance for one North London campus. Exa Infrastructure CEO Jim Fagan highlighted a "fundamental shift" in demand, with Salam's Amjad Arab stating that AI workloads can require up to 36 times more fibre than traditional applications. This demand extends beyond major hubs to local markets and enterprise sites, requiring the "whole network," euNetworks CEO Marisa Trisolino said.Long-haul and subsea capacity face significant underinvestment, according to FLAG's Paul Abfalter, leading to constraints on international routes. Sparkle CEO Enrico Bagnasco indicated that geopolitics is hindering sufficient subsea capacity development over the next five years, particularly in US and Middle East regions. Orange announced a joint venture for Pisces, a 3,125-kilometre subsea system linking Ireland, France, Spain, and Portugal.Supply chain delays are also impacting operations, with Telehouse's Ozgur Duzgunoglu reporting two-year lead times for generators and 12 to 18 months for high-voltage transformers. Greenscale's Miriam van Kooperen expressed concern about capacity, as operators commit to suppliers before design finalisation. Start Campus has adopted a "procure first, design around it" approach, with Nelson Pinto de Magalhaes measuring procurement savings in days rather than euros. Operators are also shifting to performance-based specifications to allow supplier flexibility.
### Power and Labour Constraints

Power remains a dominant constraint, with grid certainty being a larger problem than availability. An investor noted that grid operators might promise connections in 36 months but deliver in 48, burdening developers with extra capital costs. National Grid's David Atkins said the UK transmission owner is building three times more network in the current five-year period. He added that a 1 to 2 per cent flexibility from data centres could unlock significant spare capacity. Securing power in Frankfurt can take five to seven years, and anchoring a new facility in Europe takes three to four years, compared to 18 months in the US, according to Meta. This pushes operators towards behind-the-meter power solutions.Skilled labour is emerging as another critical bottleneck. Pinto de Magalhaes highlighted the difficulty of coordinating equipment, installers, and commissioning teams. Van Kooperen anticipates significant shortages in mechanical, electrical, and plumbing trades by 2029, especially in new data centre locations. Community consent is also a growing concern, with Digital Realty's Paula Cogan advocating for initiatives like Infrastructure for America to improve public understanding of data centres' local economic impact.

stories.title: NextDC cuts FY27 guidance, pauses new projects over M3 power delay
stories.summary: Australian data centre operator NextDC has sharply reduced its FY2027 revenue and earnings guidance after delays to electricity network works at its M3 Melbourne campus, with the company also pausing new development projects and land acquisitions while it reviews capital expenditure. NextDC has cut its FY2027 net revenue guidance to AU$475 million-AU$500 million, from AU$615 […]
stories.why_it_matters: The guidance cut turns grid connection timelines into a first-order financial risk for data centre operators, not just a construction detail. Landowners, contractors and investors who priced Australian capacity on the old build schedule will have to reset expectations, and other operators will scrutinise their own utility milestones more closely.
stories.content:
Australian data centre operator NextDC has sharply reduced its FY2027 revenue and earnings guidance after delays to electricity network works at its M3 Melbourne campus, with the company also pausing new development projects and land acquisitions while it reviews capital expenditure.

NextDC has cut its FY2027 net revenue guidance to AU$475 million-AU$500 million, from AU$615 million-AU$640 million previously. The revised guidance excludes the affected M3 customer contracts, including capacity already billing, because NextDC said it could not reliably estimate their FY2027 contribution amid uncertainty over power supply and contractual obligations.

Underlying EBITDA guidance has been reduced to AU$245 million-AU$265 million, down from AU$385 million-AU$410 million, according to an ASX announcement on 21 October.

The revisions primarily reflect delays to 66kV electricity network augmentation works by Jemena Electricity Networks, which supplies power to the M3 campus in Melbourne’s inner west. Jemena suspended parts of the works in September and has since advised NextDC that it does not expect them to recommence before February 2027.

Jemena has attributed the suspension to safety concerns and a lack of access to work sites amid community and stakeholder opposition, as well as the absence of local council consent for the works while further consultation takes place.

NextDC said the next increase in grid supply to M3 is now expected in FY2028, based on Jemena’s current indicative estimate. Delivery and billing of the contracted capacity dependent on that increase are expected to follow shortly afterwards.

The company had requested a trading halt on 19 October while it assessed the financial implications of the delay, including its FY2027 guidance.

### Customer contracts and potential service-level credits

The revised revenue and EBITDA guidance excludes revenue and attributable EBITDA from the affected M3 customer contracts, including capacity that is already billing and any potential service-level credits.

The company’s previous guidance, issued on 27 August, included approximately AU$140 million in net revenue and AU$140 million in underlying EBITDA from the affected contracts. NextDC said the exclusion of those contracts is the main reason for the revised guidance.

The company said it cannot yet reliably estimate the contracts’ contribution to FY2027 results. That will depend on discussions with the customer, the customer’s assessment of its contractual rights and obligations, whether NextDC can obtain relief under force majeure or other relevant provisions, and the accounting treatment of any service-level credits.

The contracts provide for service-level credits where capacity is delivered late or is not fully powered and, in some circumstances, give the customer rights to terminate. NextDC said it is assessing the potential implications of the delays under those contracts.

The company stressed that the capacity remains under contract, subject to the customer’s rights, and that construction of the data halls is continuing. It is working with the customer on a revised power ramp and with Jemena to bring forward power delivery.

NextDC chief executive and managing director Craig Scroggie said the company had removed the affected contracts from its FY2027 guidance until it could reliably estimate their contribution. “The timing and scale of their contribution remain uncertain,” Scroggie said.

NextDC added that service-level credits payable on the affected contracts could reduce underlying EBITDA below the revised guidance.

### Capital expenditure review and development pause

NextDC has also reduced its FY2027 capital expenditure guidance to AU$4.5 billion-AU$5 billion, from AU$5.25 billion-AU$5.75 billion previously, a reduction of AU$750 million, or 13%-14%. The previous guidance did not include capitalised interest.

The revised range includes approximately AU$500 million of reimbursable customer fit-out costs and AU$230 million of capitalised interest. Excluding capitalised interest, the company said the revised guidance represents a like-for-like reduction of approximately AU$980 million, or 17%-19%, from its previous range.

The reduction primarily reflects the deferral of expenditure on uncontracted data centre expansion projects, corporate technology and other projects.

NextDC said it had put all new development projects and land acquisitions on hold for the foreseeable future, focusing capital expenditure on contracted customer capacity expected to be delivered over the next 12–18 months and development work already close to completion.

The board has begun a detailed review of the capital expenditure programme and has committed to announcing its outcome by the company’s annual general meeting on 20 November. It will also evaluate capital-recycling opportunities, including the potential sale of development sites not required in the near term.

The company said that, with M3 revenue deferred, it had paused projects not backed by customer contracts and put that capital behind capacity its customers have already contracted.

### Liquidity and debt position

NextDC reported liquidity of AU$8.675 billion at 30 September 2026, comprising AU$1.275 billion in cash, AU$6.7 billion in undrawn senior debt facilities and a AU$700 million delayed-draw hybrid securities commitment, subject to customary conditions.

The company said it remained compliant with its financial covenants at the most recent test date of 30 June 2026 and expected to remain compliant at the next test date on 31 December.

However, NextDC noted that its ability to draw all undrawn senior debt facilities while remaining within covenant requirements would depend on the timing of drawdowns and the expected billing profiles of new customer contracts. It said a material change in expected customer billing profiles, including delays to M3 grid supply, could adversely affect its ability to draw senior debt.

The company said the earliest scheduled debt maturity is December 2029, although holders of its convertible notes may require redemption on 17 September 2029.

NextDC has not yet quantified the potential effect of the delays on the fair value of its investment properties. It expects to reflect any impact in its half-year results for the six months ending 31 December 2026.

### Further delays to M3 expansion approvals

The power supply delay is not the only timing issue affecting M3. NextDC said the Victorian government’s decision on a planning permit for M3 Stages 6 and 7 is taking longer than expected. The application, lodged in February 2026 under the government’s Development Facilitation Program, covers the planned expansion of the existing, partly operational campus.

With the Victorian government due to enter caretaker conventions from 3 November, ahead of the state election on 28 November, NextDC now expects the planning decision in 2027. Assuming the permit is granted, the later decision and delayed grid supply will affect the timing of delivery of the final stages of capacity at M3.

The company said later increases in grid supply also depend on upstream transmission projects to install new transformers at Brooklyn Terminal Station. NextDC now expects the first of these projects to be completed later than previously anticipated, affecting the timing of capacity expected to convert to billing after FY2028.

NextDC said it would continue working with Jemena and its customer to minimise the impact of the delays and provide further updates, including at its AGM on 20 November.

The community dispute has attracted wider attention. ABC News reported in September on residents’ objections to 15-metre power poles being installed in Melbourne’s inner west as part of network upgrades intended to support increased electricity demand, including that associated with data centres. Jemena said it had heard feedback that its communication and engagement could have been better, and that it had paused works to listen to community concerns.

NextDC said it already engages with the community around M3 through dedicated engagement staff and newsletters, and intends to build on this with a community engagement plan covering construction and operation of the campus, overseen by its board.

### NextDC withdraws Auckland consent application

Separately, **BusinessDesk in New Zealand** has reported that NextDC withdrew a resource consent application submitted to Auckland Council on 17 July for a proposed data centre site between Nelson and Hobson Streets in Auckland’s CBD.

The initial development was valued at approximately AU$140 million. The withdrawal has not been independently confirmed by other sources, and it is not known whether NextDC intends to submit a revised application or abandon the project.

stories.title: Chief Telecom breaks ground on 16MW data center in Taiwan
stories.why_it_matters: A 2028 go-live date means Chief Telecom is building into a market where Taiwan's AI supply chain — semiconductors, servers, edge — increasingly wants local compute. The 16MW addition tightens capacity supply in a compact island market where land and power are scarce, supporting pricing for existing operators.
stories.content:
Taiwanese data center and telecoms firm Chief Telecom has broken ground on a new facility.

Set on 1.5 hectares in the Central Taiwan Science Park (CTSP) Huwei Park, Huwei Township, Yunlin County, the facility is set to total 16MW across 3,335 sqm (35,897 sq ft). The data center is set to support both air-cooled and water-cooled cooling solutions.

The total investment for this project is approximately NT$3.3 billion (US$101m).

Official operations are expected in the second half of 2028.

In an August update, Chief said it had letters of intent (LOIs) signed by prospective clients exceeding 50 percent of the site’s available capacity.

Established in 1991, Chief Telecom is primarily a data center operator, with four data centers in Taipei, Taiwan’s capital. It is owned by Taiwan telecoms giant Chunghwa Telecom, and also operates cloud and networking services. The company runs the Taipei Internet eXchange (TPIX).

Chief launched its Liyuan 2 (LY2) facility in late 2024. The 20MW site totals 160,000 sq ft (14,865 sqm) of floor space across seven floors. The site reportedly offers 10-150kW per rack, supporting air and liquid cooling.
stories.title_zh: Chief Telecom 在台湾动工建设 16MW 数据中心
stories.summary_zh: 该设施预计于 2028 年投入运营
stories.why_zh: 2028年投运的日期意味着Chief Telecom正进军一个台湾AI供应链——半导体、服务器、边缘计算——日益需要本地算力的市场。这16MW的新增容量将使一个土地和电力都紧张的紧凑岛屿市场的容量供给进一步收紧，从而为现有运营商的定价提供支撑。

stories.title: Data centers explore front-of-the-meter power for grid capacity
stories.summary: Data center operators are exploring front-of-the-meter power arrangements to ease grid strain and expand capacity. This approach involves contributing electricity directly to the grid rather than solely for on-site use.
stories.content:
Data center operators, particularly large hyperscalers, are exploring front-of-the-meter power, an emerging strategy to address grid constraints and growing energy demand.This approach involves developing or supporting power generation capacity that delivers electricity to the broader grid, rather than reserving it exclusively for their own campuses. This differs from behind-the-meter generation, which serves a specific facility.The primary benefit for operators is improved electricity availability for future data center development, especially in markets facing long interconnection queues and delayed energisation timelines. By adding supply to the grid, companies may enhance their access to power as they expand.Front-of-the-meter strategies could also offer political and regulatory advantages, positioning data centers as contributors to grid capacity. This can help address concerns regarding the impact of new facilities on local power systems and electricity prices.However, developing or backing generation assets is capital-intensive, operationally complex, and subject to regulatory hurdles. For many operators, behind-the-meter infrastructure or utility partnerships may remain more practical in the near term.Amazon has been linked to a potential front-of-the-meter arrangement for a large AI data center in Texas. Public statements suggest the company is still exploring its options.Most data center operators currently rely on a mix of utility partnerships, long-term power procurement, energy storage, and behind-the-meter generation. The adoption of front-of-the-meter power will depend on grid constraints, utility expansion, and hyperscalers' strategic advantage in power development.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability
- 1 min Read

# Data centers explore front-of-the-meter power for grid capacity

Data center operators are exploring front-of-the-meter power arrangements to ease grid strain and expand capacity. This approach involves contributing electricity directly to the grid rather than solely for on-site use.

- Published On Oct 20, 2026 at 05:10 PM IST

## Highlights

- Operators are exploring front-of-the-meter power for grid capacity.
- This involves developing generation that feeds electricity directly into the grid.
- The approach aims to improve power access and address regulatory concerns.
- It is a complex strategy requiring significant capital and regulatory navigation.

# Aolani commits 500MW AI data center capacity in Malaysia

Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani signed a Letter of Intent for 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia. The firm projects a commitment of up to 580MW by 2027.

- Published On Oct 20, 2026 at 05:10 PM IST

## Highlights

- Aolani signed a Letter of Intent for 500MW of AI data center capacity in Malaysia.
- The neocloud projects a commitment of up to 580MW by 2027, up from 80MW in 2026.
- New capacity is set to come online from 2H 2027 across multiple Malaysian sites.
- Aolani will supply AI infrastructure, GPU deployment, and operating requirements.

stories.content:
Singapore-headquartered neocloud Aolani yesterday announced it has signed a Letter of Intent to take up 500 megawatt (MW) of AI data center capacity in Malaysia, with projected commitment of up to 580MW by 2027. This is up from approximately 80MW already committed in 2026, the firm said in a statement.

The capacity is targeted to come online starting in 2H 2027 across multiple sites in Malaysia. Under the arrangement, Aolani will, upon completion, supply the AI infrastructure, GPU deployment, and operating requirements. The sites will house purpose-built AI data centers to support the firm’s expansion as it meets demand from global hyperscalers and AI-native companies while also making AI compute accessible locally.

Aolani is also exploring initiatives and partnerships to provide high-performance compute capacity to Malaysian sovereign AI programmes, local enterprises, researchers and start-ups.

Nicholas Chia, Chief Executive Officer at Aolani, said: “Malaysia is a vital strategic anchor for Aolani and a proven home market where we continue to grow our footprint as a hyperlocal neocloud. Malaysia is already firmly established as a global hub for AI infrastructure, but the next stage is using local compute to catalyse development of the local AI ecosystem and the broader economy. We are committed to steering this effort, using this capacity expansion to work with local partners across the ecosystem to further democratise access to compute.”

The Letter of Intent is non-binding and is subject to execution of definitive agreements between the parties.

stories.title: ACE Market-bound SKA Capital eyes another RM500m in data centre-linked jobs to swell RM313m order book
stories.summary: Data centre-related projects account for nearly half of ACE Market-bound SKA Capital Bhd's RM313.4 million outstanding order book, as the group eyes more contracts from the fast-growing sector.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 20): Data centre-related projects account for nearly half of ACE Market-bound SKA Capital Bhd's RM313.4 million outstanding order book, as the group eyes more contracts from the fast-growing sector.

Managing director Datuk Subas Kumar Ambairam said the group is also bidding for about RM500 million worth of data centre-related projects through selective tenders.

Speaking at a press conference following the company's prospectus launch on Tuesday, he said the group has a success rate of about 25% for open tenders and between 40% and 45% for selective tenders.

Subas Kumar said continued investments in electricity infrastructure and data centre development would support demand for the group's engineering services.

"Every data centre needs a substation on a very fast-track basis," he said.

He added that even if data centre development slows, SKA Capital would continue to benefit from Tenaga Nasional Bhd's (KL:TENAGA) increased capital expenditure on electricity infrastructure.

The group expects underground utilities engineering to contribute about 30% of its revenue following the IPO, with the remaining 70% coming from substation engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) services.

SKA Capital is also seeking direct contracts from TNB through its 70%-owned subsidiary Reltency Engineering Services Sdn Bhd, while continuing to undertake civil and structural engineering works as a subcontractor.

"If the other EPCC contractors get the job, we still have a chance of getting the civil and structural works. If Reltency gets the job, we get 100% of the EPCC contract," Subas Kumar said.

He said the machinery purchases planned under the IPO would help the group execute projects more efficiently and improve margins, particularly for data centre projects that require accelerated completion.

SKA Capital's ACE Market debut is slated for Nov 11, raising over RM100 million at 43 sen per share.

stories.title: Batam data center expansion raises demand for independent water and power supplies
stories.summary: Batam’s growing data center industry is expected to require additional water and electricity infrastructure, prompting calls for operators to develop independent supplies rather than increase pressure on resources used by local residents. The infrastructure requirements extend beyond water as BP Batam estimates that existing facilities, investment commitments and planned projects represent a combined IT capacity […]
stories.content:
Batam’s growing data center industry is expected to require additional water and electricity infrastructure, prompting calls for operators to develop independent supplies rather than increase pressure on resources used by local residents. The infrastructure requirements extend beyond water as BP Batam estimates that existing facilities, investment commitments and planned projects represent a combined IT capacity of 1.47 GW, creating additional demand for reliable electricity supply.

The proposal supports BP Batam’s plan to encourage data center companies to establish their own desalination facilities in the Nongsa Special Economic Zone and Kabil industrial area. The endorsement uses Seawater Reverse Osmosis (SWRO) technology, which converts seawater into freshwater, to meet the industry’s water demand, according to a report by antaranews.

Muhammad Iftitah Sulaiman Suryanagara, Transmigration Minister, Indonesia, said, “Investment must go hand-in-hand with responsibility. Water requirements for data centers must be properly addressed, including through SWRO. The presence of data centers is not merely about technology; it also represents an opportunity for the community to secure employment, acquire skills, and earn better incomes.”

Batam has 10 data center projects in its development pipeline, including one that is already operating. The planned desalination facilities are expected to initially contribute 750 liters of water per second over the next two to three years. A subsequent expansion could raise output to 1,000 liters per second.

The expansion could strengthen Batam’s position in the global digital economy, provided infrastructure development is matched by workforce preparation and investment certainty.

The sector has already attracted major investment. In May 2026, BP Batam facilitated a US$ 5 billion project to develop an artificial intelligence data center on a 30 hectare site in Nongsa.
